needs_redesign.capability: Three-layer module topology and compile-time driver discovery (Hilt `Set<PluginFactory>` @IntoSet multibinding)
needs_redesign.why: There is no Hilt/Dagger on iOS and no compile-time multibinding mechanism in Swift. Nothing discovers conformers of a protocol at build time; Swift has no equivalent of annotation processing that assembles a set across modules. Objective-C runtime class enumeration exists but does not see pure-Swift types reliably and is a fragile, review-unfriendly hack. The three-layer separation itself (platform / driver API / drivers) maps perfectly onto SPM targets, and the ProGuard keep rules become moot (Swift is not name-minified).
options: A single explicit registration array in the app target: `let allDriverFactories: [PluginFactory] = [TandemFactory(), MedtronicFactory(), NightscoutSourceFactory(), SimulatedDriverFactory()]`. Dead simple, greppable, diff-visible, and a contributor's PR touches exactly one line plus their package.

A `DriverBundle` protocol each driver package vends, with the app target importing each package and appending its bundle. Slightly more ceremony, same explicitness, marginally better if a driver ever ships several plugins.

Objective-C runtime enumeration of conformers at launch to imitate Hilt's implicitness. Rejected: unreliable for Swift types, invisible in code review, and it makes driver load order nondeterministic.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1. SPM targets: `DriverAPI` (was `:pump-driver-api` — protocols, capability contracts, event enum, descriptors, domain models, SafetyLimits), `Platform` (was `:app` — registry, renderers, safety-limit enforcement, credential storage), and one target per driver (`TandemDriver`, `MedtronicDriver`), with the Nightscout source living in the app target for exactly the Android reason (it needs the networking + persistence + scheduling stack a driver target must not depend on). Drivers depend only on `DriverAPI`; enforce that with SPM target dependencies, which is a harder guarantee than Android's Gradle convention. Keep the explicit registration array as the single, reviewable seam. Also carry over the ID-reservation ordering: reserve each built-in driver's id before constructing it, so a transient init failure cannot leave the id claimable — cheap to keep, and it documents intent even without runtime plugins.

needs_redesign.capability: PluginRegistry (startup, derived capability slots, restore-from-preferences, runtime install/remove)
needs_redesign.why: Three changes. (1) The runtime install/remove half of the API disappears entirely (see impossible). (2) `synchronized(activationLock)` + ConcurrentHashMap needs to become Swift structured concurrency, and Android's practice of holding the activation lock across file I/O and DEX loading is a mistake not worth reproducing. (3) The biggest one: on iOS the app can be relaunched into the background by Core Bluetooth state restoration with no UI and no scene. Android calls `initialize()` from `Application.onCreate` after Timber/Sentry/networkMonitor and before auth validation; the iOS equivalent must be reachable from `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)` on a background launch, complete synchronously enough that the restored central manager's delegate callbacks find a live driver, and must not depend on any UI, scene, or authenticated backend session.
options: Make the registry an `actor` and do driver construction + restore in a launch-time `Task`. Clean, but a background BLE relaunch can deliver `willRestoreState` before the actor finishes, and the restored peripheral has nowhere to go.

Construct drivers synchronously on the main thread at `didFinishLaunchingWithOptions` (they are cheap — Android's are no-ops or DI wiring), and make only activation/deactivation actor-isolated. Restoration callbacks then always find a constructed driver.
Defer everything to first UI appearance. Rejected outright: it breaks background BLE restoration, which is the only mechanism iOS gives us in place of Android's foreground service.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. Registry construction and driver construction happen synchronously at launch, before any Core Bluetooth manager is created; activation, deactivation, and safety-limit refresh are actor-isolated. Keep `initialize()` idempotency as a hard failure on double-call (Android throws IllegalStateException — port it as a `precondition` here, because a double-initialized registry is a programmer error, not a runtime condition). Port the derived-slot resolution rules unchanged, including the deliberate `as? DevicePlugin` downcast that keeps the Nightscout source out of the pump/glucose slots. Port `restoreActivePlugins`'s subtle rules: an absent driver leaves its preference UNTOUCHED (so a gated-off driver's selection survives a later re-enable), but an onActivated *failure* clears it. `initialize()` must never require network or an auth session — the whole restore path has to work in backend-optional local mode and on a background launch.

needs_redesign.capability: DevicePlugin hardware contract (connect(address,config)/disconnect/scan/observeConnectionState, 30s timeout convention, DiscoveredDevice.address)
needs_redesign.why: Core Bluetooth differs from Android BLE in ways that reach into the data model, not just the API. (a) iOS never exposes a MAC address; you get `CBPeripheral.identifier`, a UUID that is per-app and per-device and is NOT stable across app reinstall — so a persisted 'paired address' can go dead after a reinstall even though the pump is still bonded, and it will never match across the user's phone and any other device. (b) `centralManager.connect(_:options:)` has no timeout and will retry forever, so the 'typically 30 seconds' documented convention must become real code. (c) There are no foreground services; background operation depends entirely on the `bluetooth-central` background mode plus State Preservation and Restoration (`CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey` + `centralManager(_:willRestoreState:)`), which relaunches the app into the background on a connection or notification event. (d) iOS does not require location permission for BLE (Android does), so the Android permission story shrinks — but `NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription` is mandatory or the app is killed the moment a manager is instantiated. (e) `scan()` as a completing flow maps fine, but iOS drops duplicate advertisements by default and disallows scanning with no service UUID filter while backgrounded.
options: Keep `address: String` and stuff a UUID string in it, minimizing diff from Android. Rejected: it hides a real semantic change and invites someone to try to parse or display it as a MAC.

Rename to `identifier: UUID` on `DiscoveredDevice` and `connect(identifier:config:)`, and add a documented recovery path: on launch, `retrievePeripherals(withIdentifiers:)` for the stored UUID, and if that returns nothing, `retrieveConnectedPeripherals(withServices:)` before falling back to a re-scan.

Store a driver-supplied stable device identity (pump serial number, read after connect) alongside the CBPeripheral UUID, and treat the UUID as a cache that can be re-resolved by scanning for the serial.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2 plus the serial-number backstop from option 3 where the protocol exposes one (Tandem does, via PumpSettings.serialNumber). Concretely: `DiscoveredDevice(name:identifier:rssi:driverId:metadata:)` with `identifier: UUID`; `connect(identifier:config:)` with a driver-enforced 30-second deadline that transitions to a failure state; each driver owns its own `CBCentralManager` created with a driver-scoped restore identifier, and the platform routes `willRestoreState` back to the owning driver by that identifier. Keep the 7-state `ConnectionState` and the no-platform-enforced-transition-table design exactly as-is — each driver still owns its own state machine. Keep `disconnect()` a no-op when not connected. Info.plist/entitlements this subsystem forces: `NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription`, `UIBackgroundModes: bluetooth-central`. SIMULATOR: none of this is exercisable — Core Bluetooth is absent from the iOS Simulator and the central manager reports an unsupported state, so scanning, connecting, pairing, state restoration, and every driver state machine are device-only. Plan the dev loop around a built-in simulated driver (see the contributor-path entry).

needs_redesign.capability: ADVERTISE_AND_WAIT pairing style (Medtronic MiniMed 700-series: phone is the BLE peripheral, pump connects to it as central, user selects the phone by its advertised name on the pump's own menu) and PairingFault reporting
needs_redesign.why: This is the single hardest item in the subsystem. iOS can act as a peripheral (`CBPeripheralManager`) and can advertise in the background with the `bluetooth-peripheral` mode, but background advertising is deliberately degraded: `CBAdvertisementDataLocalNameKey` is IGNORED in the background, and advertised service UUIDs are moved into a special 'overflow' area that is only discoverable by another iOS device explicitly scanning for those exact UUIDs. The Medtronic pairing flow depends on the pump seeing a human-readable local name so the user can pick the phone from the pump's menu — which means pairing can only work while the app is in the foreground with the screen on. Additionally, iOS gives no API to control the peripheral's advertised device name independently of the system device name in some contexts, and iOS's own bonding is implicit (triggered by an encrypted characteristic access) with no programmatic bond-management API. The `PairingFault` type exists precisely because advertise-and-wait failures produce no ConnectionState transition, so it remains necessary — arguably more so, since iOS surfaces fewer BLE errors than Android.
options: Foreground-attended pairing only: an explicit 'Pair MiniMed pump' screen that starts advertising, keeps the screen awake (`UIApplication.shared.isIdleTimerDisabled`), shows the advertised name the user must select on the pump, runs a visible countdown, and stops advertising on exit. Post-pairing reconnection is then whatever the pump's own reconnect behavior allows.

Foreground pairing plus background re-advertising for reconnection under `bluetooth-peripheral`, accepting the nameless overflow-area advertisement and betting the pump reconnects by bonded address rather than by scanning for a name.
Invert the topology: attempt to drive the MiniMed as a central from iOS. Rejected unless protocol work proves it viable — the Android driver's whole design says the pump insists on being central.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1 for pairing, option 2 for reconnection, and prototype this against real hardware before committing the iOS Medtronic driver to a milestone. Requirements it forces: `UIBackgroundModes: bluetooth-peripheral` in addition to `bluetooth-central`; the pairing screen must be explicitly modelled as foreground-and-attended with instructions naming the advertised device name; all five `PairingFault` values must still be surfaced to the user (unsupported, advertise failed, handshake timeout, auth failed, bound elsewhere), plus an iOS-specific sixth condition worth adding: 'pairing requires the app to stay open with the screen on'. Preserve the Android quirks: `connect` ignores the identifier entirely in this topology, and `scan()` emits a device only after the pump has connected. Do not reproduce Android's `forceFirstPair` config key as a raw string map — model connect config as a typed per-driver struct. SIMULATOR: fully unexercisable; CBPeripheralManager is as absent as CBCentralManager.

needs_redesign.capability: Shipped reference drivers' polling model (`GlucoseSource.observeReadings()` implemented as `flow { while(true) { poll(); delay(60_000) } }` in both Tandem and Medtronic)
needs_redesign.why: An unbounded `while true { try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(60)) }` does not run on iOS. Once the app is suspended, the task simply stops and resumes at an arbitrary later time with an unbounded gap and no notification that it stalled. Android relies on a `connectedDevice`-typed foreground service to keep this loop alive; iOS has no foreground services at all. Compounding it, both Android drivers swallow poll failures via `onSuccess` with no backoff and no error surface, which on iOS would make an indefinitely stalled feed indistinguishable from a healthy one.
options: Keep timer polling but run it only while the app is foreground/active, and rely on the freshness policy to mark data stale when backgrounded. Honest, but it means glucose stops updating whenever the phone is in a pocket — a monitoring-app regression.

Move to event-driven ingestion: subscribe to BLE characteristic notifications where the protocol offers them, so the OS wakes the app on each notification under `bluetooth-central`, and treat polling as a catch-up performed on each wake rather than as the primary mechanism.

Hybrid: event-driven where available, plus an opportunistic catch-up poll on every background wake (BLE event, BGAppRefreshTask, foreground entry), plus a foreground timer for live-view responsiveness.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 3, and change the driver contract to make it explicit: `observeReadings()` returns a stream the driver feeds from device events, and the platform separately calls a `catchUp()`/`getCurrentReading()` on each wake. Do not let a driver own a wall-clock cadence — Android's own code comments already say cadence ownership moves to the polling orchestrator, so this port should land there directly rather than inheriting the interim `while(true)` shape. Add what Android lacks: bounded backoff on repeated failures and a surfaced last-successful-read timestamp per driver, so a stalled feed is visible rather than silent. Note that both Tandem and Medtronic will need BLE-level rework anyway (per-driver `CBCentralManager`, restore identifiers, UUID-not-MAC identity), and Medtronic additionally needs the peripheral-role work above; the driver *shape* (thin capability delegates over a BLE layer, per-driver bolus cursor under a mutex, drop-not-clamp on over-cap boluses, `shutdown()` fully tearing down vs `onDeactivated()` merely disconnecting) all ports unchanged.

needs_redesign.capability: PluginContext (what the platform hands a driver)
needs_redesign.why: `androidContext: Context` has no iOS analogue and its two real jobs must be replaced by explicit, narrower grants: access to Bluetooth hardware, and access to a place to put files. On iOS the hardware grant is a `CBCentralManager`/`CBPeripheralManager`, and there is a genuine architectural question about who owns those managers because state restoration requires a unique, stable restore identifier per manager and iOS restores every one of them at launch.
options: Each driver creates its own CBCentralManager privately and the context grants nothing. Simplest, but the platform then cannot route `willRestoreState` at launch, and a driver constructed lazily would miss its own restoration callback.

The platform vends a single shared CBCentralManager to all drivers and demultiplexes delegate callbacks. Rejected: delegate demuxing across drivers with different service UUIDs and different scan filters is a bug farm, and one driver's `stopScan` clobbers another's.

The context vends a factory: `func makeCentralManager(restoreIdentifier:delegate:) -> CBCentralManager`. The platform records the identifier, guarantees the owning driver is constructed before Core Bluetooth is touched at launch, and routes restoration to it.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 3. `PluginContext` becomes a Swift struct with: `pluginId`, `settingsStore`, `credentialStore` (Keychain-backed, see below), `debugLogger`, `eventBus`, `safetyLimits` (a live value, always current), `apiVersion`, and `bluetooth` (the manager factory). Drop `androidContext` entirely and drop the restricted-vs-full context distinction — with only compile-time drivers there is one context flavor, which removes an entire class of Android complexity. Preserve the DebugLogger contract verbatim including its security clause: TX/RX packet direction, opcode, txId, cargo hex, parsed value, error — retained only in debug builds and never persisted unencrypted, because cargo can contain glucose values, insulin doses, and device identifiers.

needs_redesign.capability: Credential storage (PumpCredentialProvider on EncryptedSharedPreferences; ScopedCredentialProvider on plain SharedPreferences for runtime plugins)
needs_redesign.why: Keychain is not SharedPreferences with encryption bolted on; three behaviors differ in ways that matter. (1) Accessibility class: the default `WhenUnlocked` would make pump pairing secrets unreadable during a background Bluetooth wake on a locked phone, breaking auto-reconnect exactly when it matters. (2) Keychain items SURVIVE app deletion on iOS — delete and reinstall the app and stale pump pairing credentials are still there, which Android's model never produces. (3) iCloud Keychain would sync pump pairing secrets to the user's other devices unless explicitly prevented. Separately, the entire ScopedCredentialProvider isolation mechanism and its documented accepted risk (runtime plugins can't reach AndroidX Security, so their credentials sit in plaintext prefs) evaporate, because there is no untrusted in-process code to isolate from.
options: One Keychain service per driver id (`<bundleid>.driver.<pluginId>`) with the same four logical items (paired identifier, pairing code, JPAKE derived secret, JPAKE server nonce). Preserves Android's namespacing intent with a strictly stronger store.

One Keychain item per driver holding a Codable credential blob. Fewer items, atomic multi-field writes (savePairing writes address+code together; the JPAKE pair is saved and cleared together — both are already atomic pairs on Android).
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2, with `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` — `AfterFirstUnlock` so background BLE reconnect works on a locked device, `ThisDeviceOnly` so pump pairing secrets never leave the phone via iCloud Keychain or an encrypted backup. Add a first-run purge: on launch, if a 'keychain initialized' flag is absent from UserDefaults (which IS wiped on app deletion), clear all driver credential items — this closes the survives-deletion gap and also fixes the Android bug where removing a plugin deleted its settings but left `plugin_creds_<id>` behind. Keep the id-sanitization rule that preserves dots/hyphens/underscores so `com.foo.bar-baz` and `com.foo.bar.baz` stay distinct namespaces. Related storage decision for this subsystem: the readings database the Nightscout mapper writes into must use file protection `CompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication` (not `Complete`), or background ingestion on a locked device fails; add SQLCipher only if the threat model expands to physical device extraction, and note it is not needed to protect against another app (the iOS sandbox already does that, unlike the Android threat model that motivated EncryptedSharedPreferences). SIMULATOR: Keychain works but is not Secure-Enclave backed and the simulated device is effectively always unlocked, so `AfterFirstUnlock`-vs-`WhenUnlocked` behavior cannot be distinguished there — that distinction must be verified on a real locked device.

needs_redesign.capability: Fail-fast invariant enforcement (Kotlin `require`/`check` throwing catchable IllegalArgumentException in CgmReading, BgmReading, BolusEvent, SafetyLimits, CalibrationRequested, and every UI descriptor)
needs_redesign.why: This is the highest-consequence translation decision in the subsystem and it is easy to get silently wrong. Android's invariants throw catchable exceptions, and the platform *relies* on catching them: SettingsViewModel wraps `metadata` and `settingsDescriptor()` in `try/catch(Throwable)` specifically so a misbehaving plugin degrades instead of crashing. Swift has no catchable equivalent — `precondition`, `assert`, and `fatalError` trap the process and cannot be recovered from. A literal transcription of `require(...)` into `precondition(...)` converts 'this driver's reading was rejected' into 'the glucose monitoring app crash-loops'. Going the other way and clamping is explicitly called out in the map as the worse failure: it turns a loud driver bug into a wrong number on a glucose chart.
options: `precondition` everywhere (literal transcription). Rejected: process traps in a monitoring app, and untestable — XCTest cannot assert on a trap.
Throwing initializers everywhere (`init(glucoseMgDl:...) throws`), forcing every call site to handle rejection explicitly. Verbose but total, and directly testable with `XCTAssertThrowsError`.
Failable initializers returning nil. Concise, but nil loses the reason and invites `if let` chains that silently skip records without logging which limit was violated.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2 for every value that can originate from a device, the backend, or a driver: `CgmReading`, `BgmReading`, `BolusEvent`, `SafetyLimits`'s strict init, `CalibrationRequested`, and all UI descriptors. Reserve `precondition` strictly for programmer errors that cannot occur at runtime with valid input — double-initializing the registry is the only real instance in this subsystem, and the capability-exhaustiveness check becomes a compile-time exhaustive switch and disappears entirely. The behavioral contract to preserve: construction of an out-of-range reading must FAIL — never clamp, never silently drop without a logged reason naming the violated limit. Where Android caught Throwable around `metadata`/`settingsDescriptor()`, Swift needs no equivalent for compile-time drivers (there are no linkage errors), but keep the descriptor accessors `throws` so a driver that computes an invalid descriptor degrades to 'no notes shown' rather than taking down Settings — and preserve Android's deliberate split where a descriptor failure drops only the informational notes while keeping the pump card, since losing metadata necessarily drops the card.

needs_redesign.capability: PluginMetadata and API versioning (PLUGIN_API_VERSION = 5, exact-equality enforcement at registry init and JAR load, silent skip on mismatch)
needs_redesign.why: With compile-time-only linking, every driver is compiled against the same `DriverAPI` headers in the same build, so a runtime version mismatch is structurally impossible. Keeping the runtime check as-is would be dead code whose only possible effect is catastrophic: a shipped driver silently vanishing from the driver list with nothing but a log line. Android already demonstrates the failure mode — the shipped example plugin's manifest declares apiVersion 1 against a constant of 5 and would be rejected today, and the architecture doc still says 2.
options: Delete the version constant entirely. Clean, but loses the documented compatibility contract that out-of-tree forks and the plugin-development docs depend on.

Keep the constant as a source-compatibility marker and enforce it with a unit test that asserts every registered driver's declared apiVersion equals the constant, so a mismatch fails CI rather than silently dropping a driver at runtime.
Keep the runtime check with a user-visible error state ('Driver X could not be loaded') instead of a silent skip.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2, plus keep the semantic rules unchanged (bump on breaking changes to the driver protocol, capability protocols, context members, event cases, or descriptor cases; no bump for additive changes) and keep the documented changelog. Reset the constant deliberately for the iOS SDK rather than inheriting 5 — and do NOT carry over the doc drift (docs say 2, code says 5, example manifest says 1) or the missing entries (docs omit BOLUS_CATEGORY_PROVIDER, `getFullHistoryLogs`, PairingProfile/PairingFault, the detail-screen API). Keep the `protocolName` + `version` display convention ('Tandem v1.0.0') and the rule that the driver's `version` doubles as its protocol version. Keep the driver-id regex `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._-]{1,127}$` because it still guards UserDefaults suite names and Keychain service names.

needs_redesign.capability: Nightscout background scheduling (WorkManager: 15-minute unique periodic work + one-shot REPLACE, NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint, exponential retry backoff, stand-down when no backend)
needs_redesign.why: iOS has nothing that guarantees a 15-minute cadence, and no foreground service to fall back on. `BGAppRefreshTask`'s `earliestBeginDate` is a hint the scheduler is free to ignore; actual delivery is driven by usage patterns and can be zero if the user rarely opens the app, if Background App Refresh is off, or if Low Power Mode is on. `BGProcessingTask` gets minutes instead of ~30 seconds but typically wants the device idle and charging, so it is even less predictable. Silent push (`content-available`) is the only server-driven option and is itself throttled by iOS and suppressed in Low Power Mode — and it requires the backend to hold APNs credentials scoped to this app's Team ID, which a self-hoster cannot obtain. Live Activities are a display surface and grant no background execution; they cannot be used to keep the sync loop alive.
options: BGAppRefreshTask only, with a 15-minute earliestBeginDate as a best-effort hint. Simple, honest, and can starve completely.

Layered opportunistic triggers: foreground/scene-active sync, pull-to-refresh, BGAppRefreshTask, plus a sync on every Core Bluetooth background wake (which is frequent whenever a BLE driver is connected, and is the mechanism iOS diabetes apps actually rely on).

Layered as above plus optional silent push when the operator has APNs configured — near-real-time when available, unavailable in backend-optional local mode and for self-hosters without APNs credentials.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2 as the baseline, with option 3's push trigger designed for but gated behind an explicit operator capability (see the one PM question). Concretely: register a `BGAppRefreshTaskRequest` with `earliestBeginDate = now + 15min` and reschedule at the START of every handler run (a handler that forgets to reschedule permanently kills the cadence); sync on scene-active; sync opportunistically on any background BLE wake; expose an explicit 'Sync now'. Preserve the Android semantics that still apply: the enable flag persists across a backend stand-down so sync resumes when a backend reappears; `disable()` cancels the schedule but retains cached data; the stand-down cancels any orphaned schedule left from a previous full-stack life. Replace the network constraint with an in-handler reachability check plus `waitsForConnectivity` on the URLSession config. Replace WorkManager's `Result.retry()` + exponential backoff with an explicit reschedule-sooner on transient outcomes. Info.plist this forces: `UIBackgroundModes: fetch` (and `processing` if a longer backfill task is added), plus `BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers` listing every task id — a task id missing from that array throws at registration. Most important product requirement: the UI must never imply freshness the platform did not deliver. The existing design already carries this correctly (last-sync timestamp, status badges, and a freshness policy keyed on the reading's capture timestamp), and that must be treated as load-bearing on iOS rather than cosmetic. SIMULATOR: BGTaskScheduler does not fire on its own schedule in the Simulator (or dependably on device); trigger handlers via the debugger's `_simulateLaunchForTaskWithIdentifier:` to validate correctness, and use a real device to observe cadence. `xcrun simctl push` can deliver a silent push to the Simulator, so the push-triggered path is testable in shape but not in throttling behavior.

needs_redesign.capability: NightscoutSyncWorker execution shell (CoroutineWorker.doWork, cancellation rethrown, Transient->retry, never returns failure)
needs_redesign.why: A `BGAppRefreshTask` handler gets roughly 30 seconds of wall clock and is killed hard if it does not call `setTaskCompleted(success:)` in time — and repeated expirations cause iOS to throttle future scheduling for the app. The Android paging loop it wraps has NO iteration cap and no timeout ('the whole sync runs inside doWork with no explicit timeout'), which is survivable under WorkManager and is not survivable here. A full backfill from cursor 0 over 500-row pages can easily exceed 30 seconds.
options: Run the same unbounded loop and hope it finishes. Rejected: expiration kills it mid-page, iOS throttles the app, and repeated partial runs never converge.

Bound each background run by a wall-clock deadline (~20s, leaving headroom) and an iteration cap, persist the cursor after every successful page, and let the next run resume. Requires per-page cursor persistence rather than persist-once-at-the-end.
Do full backfills only in the foreground or in a `BGProcessingTask`, and restrict `BGAppRefreshTask` runs to incremental catch-up.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Options 2 and 3 together. Change the engine to persist the cursor after every page (Android persists only on loop exit and on the stall guard), add both a deadline and an iteration cap to the loop, and wire `task.expirationHandler` to cancel the sync task cooperatively — Swift's cooperative cancellation maps directly onto Android's rethrow-CancellationException rule, and cancellation must never be swallowed into a retry. Preserve the outcome mapping's intent: `Disabled`, `NoBackend`, `NoConnection`, `Success` and `AuthError` are all terminal for the run (retrying cannot help until the user acts) and only `Transient` requests a sooner reschedule; always call `setTaskCompleted` on every path. Route a first-run full backfill to the foreground or a `BGProcessingTask` so it is never attempted inside a 30-second window.

needs_redesign.capability: Self-hosted backend reachability for the Nightscout source (App Transport Security and Local Network privacy)
needs_redesign.why: Verified in the Android repo: `network_security_config.xml` sets `cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"` in base-config specifically so users can point the app at a self-hosted LAN backend over plain HTTP (the app even has an 'insecure-HTTP indicator' for this case). iOS blocks that by default under ATS, and separately, since iOS 14, ANY connection to a local-network address — including a bare `http://192.168.1.x:8000` — triggers the Local Network privacy prompt and requires `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`, or the connection silently fails. Neither restriction has an Android equivalent, and both land squarely on the Nightscout source's ability to reach its backend in the self-hosted and backend-optional modes this project targets.
options: Require HTTPS with a publicly trusted certificate for all backends. Cleanest for App Review, but excludes the plain-LAN self-hoster the Android app explicitly supports.

Declare `NSAllowsLocalNetworking = YES` (permits cleartext to link-local, .local, and RFC1918 addresses without a blanket exception and without the App Review justification that `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads` attracts) plus `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`, and require HTTPS for anything off-LAN.
Declare `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = YES`. Rejected: it invites an App Review justification request even for TestFlight beta review, and it disables ATS for genuinely remote hosts where it should apply.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. It preserves the Android capability (LAN self-hosting over HTTP) with the narrowest possible exception, and it maps cleanly onto the app's existing insecure-HTTP indicator, which should be carried over so the user can see when their connection is unencrypted. Anything not on the local network must be HTTPS — document that plainly for self-hosters and point at the standard remedies (a reverse proxy with a real certificate, or a private overlay network). Also preserve `isBackendConfigured()` (non-blank base URL) as the single switch for backend-optional local mode, and preserve every behavior it gates: the sync engine's `NoBackend` terminal, status-free outcome; the manager's stand-down that cancels orphaned schedules; and the Settings rule that hides the Nightscout activation control entirely when no backend is configured unless it is already active. SIMULATOR: the Local Network privacy prompt does NOT appear in the iOS Simulator (it uses the Mac's network stack), so a LAN backend that works perfectly in the Simulator can fail on the first real device with no obvious error. This must be on the device test matrix explicitly.

needs_redesign.capability: Settings > Plugins UI (Available Plugins list, activate/deactivate with confirmation, Custom Plugins card with install/remove and trust warning)
needs_redesign.why: The Available Plugins half ports directly; the Custom Plugins half has nothing to render because runtime plugin installation is impossible on iOS. Leaving an empty or disabled card would be worse than removing it.
options: Remove the Custom Plugins card entirely and say nothing.

Remove the card and add a read-only 'Included drivers' section listing each compiled-in driver with its version, protocol name, and build-gate state, so the information the Custom Plugins card used to carry (what is installed, at what version) still has a home.
Keep an install affordance pointing at documentation for building a fork. Rejected: it dead-ends the user in a way the Android UI never did.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. Keep everything else verbatim: the derived `visibleAvailablePlugins` rule (computed in the state type so it can never go stale, hiding the Nightscout activation control in BLE-only mode unless already active), name + version per row, activate/deactivate buttons, the mandatory deactivate confirmation naming the consequences ('may stop glucose monitoring, insulin tracking, or other services it provides'), and the pump pairing card shown whenever any pump driver is active with only the active driver's InfoText notes surfaced (never its interactive settings, since the pump card owns live pairing status and pair/unpair). The 'not verified by GlycemicGPT / only install from sources you trust' warning goes away with the mechanism it warned about — every driver in an iOS build is signed and reviewed as part of the app.

needs_redesign.capability: Legacy adapters (PumpDriverAdapter, PumpConnectionAdapter, PumpScannerAdapter, HistoryLogParserAdapter bridging the registry onto four deprecated pump interfaces)
needs_redesign.why: These exist solely as Android migration scaffolding — they let pre-plugin consumers compile unchanged against interfaces already marked @Deprecated. A greenfield Swift app has no such consumers, so porting them would import dead abstraction plus two live defects.
options: Port them faithfully for structural parity. Rejected: they are explicitly deprecated in the source they come from.
Skip them and have consumers resolve capabilities through the registry's derived slots directly.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2, and deliberately do not recreate the two defects they carry. First, `HistoryLogParserAdapter` returns an empty list rather than an error when no driver is active, so a caller cannot distinguish 'the patient had no boluses' from 'no driver is installed' — on iOS make 'no active driver' a distinct typed error on every capability read (Android's `NoActivePluginException` already exists for the other adapters and should be the uniform answer). Second, `PumpDriverAdapter.getCgmStatus` reads the glucose-source slot while every other read goes through the pump slot, which silently mixes two different drivers when a CGM-only driver runs alongside a pump — make the slot each read targets explicit at the call site. Do port the useful semantics: connection state that follows the active pump driver reactively, an empty scan stream when no driver is active, and cancellation propagating rather than being converted to a failure.

needs_redesign.capability: Community contributor path (compile-time Gradle module PR, plus the runtime JAR path and the plugins/example reference plugin)
needs_redesign.why: The endorsed compile-time path translates almost directly (a driver becomes an SPM package + one line in the registration array + a PR), but the runtime path is gone, and with it the ability for a non-developer to try a community driver. On iOS, running an unshipped driver requires cloning the repo, opening Xcode, and signing with your own Apple ID (a free account yields a 7-day provisioning profile; a paid account, one year). That is a materially higher bar than `adb push` into files/plugins, and it must be stated rather than glossed. The reference example plugin also cannot exist as a loadable artifact.
options: Compile-time PR path only, plus a documented fork-and-build guide for developers who want to run an unmerged driver on their own device.

The above, plus a data-driven driver descriptor (JSON/plist describing GATT services, characteristics, and field layouts) interpreted by a built-in generic BLE engine — data, not executable code, so it does not violate the downloaded-code rule.
Convert the example plugin into a first-class shipped simulated driver.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Options 1 and 3 for v1; treat option 2 as a later exploration and be honest about its ceiling — a descriptor language cannot express Tandem's or Medtronic's authenticated handshakes (JPAKE, pairing codes, sequence-cursored history logs), so it would only ever cover trivial notify-only meters and is not a substitute for the runtime path. Option 3 is the important one and is not merely a consolation prize: because Core Bluetooth does not exist in the iOS Simulator, a compiled-in `SimulatedDriver` — the direct descendant of Android's DemoGlucometerPlugin, declaring the same deliberately non-conflicting multi-instance capabilities (BGM_SOURCE + DATA_SYNC), publishing the same events, exercising every card element and every lifecycle hook, and validating each fabricated reading against the live safety limits re-read on every iteration — is what makes the entire Simulator development loop possible. Port its simulator math (base 130 + 50·sin(phase), ±10 jitter, 2π/12 phase step, clamp to 20...500, 12-reading history, 30s default interval with a 5–300s slider at step 5) and, critically, its drop-out-of-range-with-a-log behavior. Gate it behind the feature gate so it can be excluded from production builds while remaining available in TestFlight if desired. Contributor docs must also cover what Android's do not: the required Info.plist keys and background modes a new BLE driver forces, and the fact that a driver's BLE code cannot be tested in the Simulator at all.

impossible.capability: Runtime plugin loading and execution (DexPluginLoader: DexClassLoader over sideloaded JARs, manifest-driven reflective factory instantiation, discovery from filesDir/plugins/*.jar at startup)
impossible.why: Apple forbids it at two independent levels. App Store Review Guideline 2.5.2 requires that apps be self-contained and prohibits reading or writing data outside their container and downloading, installing, or executing code that introduces or changes features — and this applies to TestFlight builds too (external-tester builds go through Beta App Review, and the Developer Program License Agreement clause the guideline derives from applies regardless of distribution channel). Independently, the OS enforces it: iOS requires every executable page to be backed by code signed at build time by the developer's certificate, there is no writable-executable memory outside the dynamic-codesigning entitlement that only WebKit holds, and `dlopen` only succeeds for frameworks already embedded and signed inside the app bundle. There is no workaround, no entitlement to request, and no enterprise or TestFlight carve-out.
impossible.closest_alternative: Compile-time-linked Swift driver packages, which is the decision already made. A contributor's driver ships to users only by being merged and included in the next TestFlight build; a developer can run an unmerged driver on their own device by building the fork in Xcode with their own signing identity. If a lightweight extension path is ever wanted, the only lawful version is a purely declarative, non-executable driver descriptor (a JSON/plist GATT map) interpreted by an engine already compiled into the app — that is data, not code, so it is permitted, but it cannot express any protocol requiring an authenticated handshake, so it would not cover either shipped driver.

impossible.capability: Runtime plugin package install and removal (PluginFileManager: SAF file-picker install of a .jar, 50 MB cap, ZIP-magic validation, canonical-path containment, setReadOnly for DexClassLoader; plus the Custom Plugins add/remove UI and its trust warning)
impossible.why: This machinery exists only to place executable code on disk for DexClassLoader to run. With runtime execution forbidden, an install flow has nothing to install into. Copying an arbitrary file into the app container via UIDocumentPicker is technically possible on iOS, but a file that can never be executed serves no purpose, and shipping an 'Add Plugin' button that produces an inert file would be user-hostile and would likely itself draw review attention under 2.5.2.
impossible.closest_alternative: Remove the flow entirely and replace the Custom Plugins card with a read-only 'Included drivers' list (name, version, protocol, build-gate state), so the information the card conveyed — what drivers this build contains and at what version — still has a home. The trust warning becomes unnecessary because every driver in an iOS build is signed and reviewed as part of the app binary.

impossible.capability: PluginManifest (META-INF/plugin.json: factoryClass, apiVersion, id, name, version, author, description; parse-order-sensitive validation, 65,536-char size cap, resource-shadowing hazard)
impossible.why: A manifest is the metadata half of a loadable code artifact. With no loadable artifact there is no manifest, no factory class name to reflect on, no independent id that can diverge from the driver's own metadata, and no resource-stream shadowing hazard. Reflective instantiation from a class-name string is additionally not something Swift supports for pure-Swift types.
impossible.closest_alternative: The driver's `PluginMetadata`, declared in Swift and constructed at compile time, is the single source of truth — which also permanently eliminates the Android hazard where a manifest id and a metadata id disagree and the registry keys on one while the UI displays the other. The manifest's apiVersion field becomes a CI-enforced assertion rather than a parsed value.

impossible.capability: RestrictedPluginContext / RestrictedContext in-process sandbox (ContextWrapper subclass blocking ~30 methods: startActivity/startService/bindService, getContentResolver, sendBroadcast/registerReceiver, getSharedPreferences, file and database APIs, createPackageContext, device-protected storage; getApplicationContext trapped to return itself; allowlisted getSystemService set of BLUETOOTH/LOCATION/POWER/ALARM/SENSOR/USB/WIFI with WINDOW deliberately excluded)
impossible.why: The sandbox is a language-level wrapper whose entire purpose is to constrain untrusted third-party code running in-process. On iOS there is no untrusted in-process code — every line in the binary was compiled and signed by the project — so the threat model it addresses does not exist. It is also unbuildable in principle: there is no `Context` object to wrap, iOS APIs are reached through global singletons and framework types that no wrapper can interpose on, and Swift has no mechanism to deny a linked module access to `CBCentralManager` or `FileManager`. Android's own docs already record that this sandbox is porous (a plugin can reflect over host classes to bypass it) and that true process isolation was considered and rejected as too complex.
impossible.closest_alternative: The iOS trust boundary moves from runtime enforcement to code review plus SPM target dependencies. Driver targets depend only on `DriverAPI` and cannot import the platform target, which is a *compile-time* guarantee stronger than anything RestrictedContext provided at runtime. The safety guarantee that actually mattered survives intact and unchanged: enforcement comes from SafetyLimits and the absence of any therapeutic write in the SDK surface, not from Context restrictions — Android's own stated design philosophy. The credential-isolation goal that ScopedCredentialProvider served (and its documented accepted risk of plaintext SharedPreferences for runtime plugins) is superseded outright by per-driver Keychain namespacing for all drivers, which is strictly stronger than what either Android path had.

ios_requirements: The app must ship with every supported pump and CGM driver compiled into the signed binary; the user must be able to see every driver the build contains without installing anything, and must never be offered a way to add a driver at runtime.
The user must be able to view a list of available drivers showing name and version, and activate or deactivate each one.

Activating a driver that claims a single-instance capability (glucose source, insulin source, pump status, calibration target, bolus-category provider) must automatically deactivate the previously active driver for that capability, and the capability slot must never be momentarily empty during the swap.
Multiple blood-glucose-meter sources and multiple data-sync sources must be able to be active at the same time; activating a cloud data source must never evict an active pump or CGM driver.
Deactivating a driver must require an explicit confirmation that names the consequences (may stop glucose monitoring, insulin tracking, or other services it provides).

The user's driver selection must survive app relaunch, device restart, and app upgrade, and must be restored automatically at launch — including a launch the system triggers in the background because of a Bluetooth event, with no user interface and no network available.

A driver disabled by a build-time kill switch must be entirely absent from the driver list and must never run, and re-enabling it in a later build must restore the user's prior selection without the user re-choosing it.

A driver that fails to initialize must be skipped without preventing any other driver from loading and without crashing the app; a driver that fails while being activated must not be recorded as active.
Each driver must have private, namespaced settings storage that survives deactivation and reactivation, app upgrade, and background operation while the device is locked.

Pump pairing secrets (device identifier, pairing code, derived handshake secrets) must be stored in the iOS Keychain, must remain readable during a background Bluetooth wake while the device is locked, must never sync to iCloud or leave the device in a backup, and must be purged automatically on a fresh install following app deletion.

The app must let the user pair with a pump the phone discovers by scanning, showing each discovered device's name and signal strength, letting the user cancel the scan, and failing a connection attempt within a bounded time rather than retrying indefinitely.

The app must let the user pair with a pump that connects to the phone rather than the reverse. This flow must be presented as a foreground, screen-on, user-attended pairing session that tells the user the exact name to select on the pump's own pairing menu and keeps the screen awake for its duration.

When an advertise-and-wait pairing fails, the app must show a specific reason — device does not support this mode, advertising failed, handshake timed out, authentication failed, or the pump is already paired to another phone — even though no connection state change occurs.
Connection state must be surfaced to the user across at least: disconnected, scanning, connecting, authenticating, authentication failed, connected, and reconnecting.
After the system terminates and relaunches the app in the background, the app must reconnect to a previously paired device and resume data collection without the user re-pairing.

When a stored device identifier no longer resolves (for example after an app reinstall), the app must attempt recovery before asking the user to re-pair, and must tell the user plainly if re-pairing is required.

Drivers must expose no therapeutic write of any kind. The driver SDK must contain no bolus delivery, no basal change, and no pump-setting write; connect, disconnect, calibrate, unpair, and reconnect must be the only operations that touch the device.

Every glucose value entering the system must be rejected — never clamped, never silently corrected — if it falls outside 20–500 mg/dL, at reading construction, at cloud ingestion, at calibration request, and at calibration validation.
Every bolus must be rejected outside 0–25 units; every basal rate ingested from the cloud must be rejected outside 0–15 units/hour; non-finite values must be rejected by an explicit finiteness check.
Rejection of an out-of-range record must be recoverable and logged with the limit that was violated; it must never terminate the app and must never write a corrected value.
Safety limits supplied by the backend must only ever narrow the absolute clinical bounds; a value that would widen them must be clamped on write and clamped again on read, and must never take effect.

Safety limits must be persisted as a single atomic record and must be available to every driver as a live value that updates as soon as the backend refreshes them; drivers must read them fresh on every use rather than caching a snapshot.

Any read of pump history, status, or insulin data while no driver is active must return a result the caller can distinguish from a genuine empty result — the app must never present 'no driver installed' as 'the patient had no boluses'.

The user must be able to enable a cloud data source that pulls their Nightscout-derived glucose and insulin from their own backend account into the same local store the Bluetooth drivers write into, without a second Nightscout client on the device.

The cloud data source must be off by default, must retain already-synced data when disabled, and must not be offerable at all when no backend is configured — unless it is already active, in which case turning it off must remain reachable.

The cloud data source must show the time of the last successful sync and a distinct state for each of: never synced, healthy, no Nightscout connection configured, re-authentication required, and sync error that will be retried. The last successful sync time must remain visible even while an error state is shown.
The user must be able to trigger an immediate sync on demand and see the sync state update without leaving the screen.

When the user's account has more than one active Nightscout connection, the user must be able to choose which one syncs; when only one exists no choice may be presented; and if the chosen connection is deleted or deactivated the app must report that there is no connection rather than silently syncing a different one.

Background sync must be best-effort and the interface must never imply a freshness the platform did not deliver: staleness shown to the user must be derived from each reading's real capture time, not from when the app fetched it, so a frozen cloud feed ages out exactly like a frozen Bluetooth feed.

A background sync run must finish within the time the system grants it or abort cleanly, persisting the progress it made so the next run resumes from the same point; it must never skip, lose, or double-count records, and a first-time full backfill must not be attempted inside a short background window.

Records that arrive at the same timestamp from a cloud source and a Bluetooth driver must collapse to a single record with a deterministic, documented winner per data type, so no dose or reading is ever counted twice.
The app must run usefully with no backend configured: driver activation, pairing, Bluetooth data collection, dashboard display, and local storage must all work without a server.

The app must be able to reach a self-hosted backend on the user's local network, must ask for local network access with a clear explanation, and must show the user when their connection to that backend is unencrypted.

Logs must never contain glucose values, insulin doses, or backend connection credentials; raw device packet captures may exist only in non-release builds and must never be written to disk unencrypted.
Drivers must be able to contribute dashboard cards and a tappable detail screen built entirely from a fixed set of declarative elements the platform renders; no driver may supply view code.

Plugin card ordering must be deterministic across refreshes, with platform cards above driver cards, and driver-supplied content must not be able to degrade or hang the interface (nesting beyond five levels and detail screens beyond one hundred elements must be refused).
A setting the user types must be persisted when they leave the field or leave the screen, never silently discarded by navigating away.

The Apple Watch app must not host drivers and must not perform device pairing; it must display data the phone has already collected. Driver management, pairing, plugin cards, and plugin detail screens are phone-only surfaces.

The app must include a built-in simulated data source that produces realistic, safety-limit-validated readings and exercises the full driver lifecycle, card rendering, settings persistence, and detail screens, so the entire driver-management experience can be developed and validated in the iOS Simulator without hardware. It must be excludable from production builds.

The app must declare its active driver's bolus-category vocabulary and its mapping to platform categories to the backend when a driver becomes active, and must clear that declaration when no driver or no category provider is active; failure to do so must never block driver activation.

risks.risk: Medtronic advertise-and-wait pairing may be unachievable on iOS. The flow requires the pump to discover the phone by a human-readable advertised name, but iOS never advertises a local name while backgrounded and pushes service UUIDs into an overflow area readable only by iOS devices scanning for them explicitly. Even foreground advertising gives less control over the advertised identity than Android does. If the MiniMed 7xx firmware will not accept an iOS peripheral's advertisement, Medtronic support on iOS is blocked outright and the parity mandate cannot be met for that device.
risks.mitigation: Prototype CBPeripheralManager against real MiniMed hardware as the very first iOS driver task, ahead of any UI work — this is the single highest-variance unknown in the subsystem. Design the pairing screen as explicitly foreground-and-attended with the screen kept awake. If the pump will not connect, the honest fallback is Medtronic-via-cloud only (Nightscout source or backend Medtronic integration), which must be surfaced to the user as a different capability, not as a degraded pairing.

risks.risk: Nightscout cloud-source freshness will be materially worse than Android's. WorkManager guarantees a 15-minute floor; BGAppRefreshTask guarantees nothing, can be starved entirely for users who rarely open the app or who have Background App Refresh off or Low Power Mode on, and gives roughly 30 seconds when it does run. Users on the cloud source with no Bluetooth device connected have no background wake source at all, so their data can be hours stale with the app appearing healthy.
risks.mitigation: Layer the triggers (foreground, pull-to-refresh, background app refresh, and opportunistic sync on every Bluetooth background wake), and treat the freshness UI as load-bearing rather than cosmetic: the last-sync timestamp and the capture-time-based staleness policy must make a stalled feed visibly stalled. Do not ship copy that promises a sync interval. Consider a first-run explanation of iOS background limits for cloud-source-only users.

risks.risk: A literal transcription of Kotlin `require`/`check` into Swift `precondition` would turn every recoverable validation failure into a process trap. In a glucose monitoring app this converts 'one bad record was rejected' into a crash loop, potentially during a background Bluetooth wake where the user never sees why. The inverse mistake — clamping to avoid the trap — is worse still, silently fabricating a plausible glucose or dose value on a chart the patient reads.
risks.mitigation: Make throwing initializers the mandated pattern for every value originating from a device, a driver, or the backend, and forbid `precondition` outside genuine programmer errors. Carry the Android unit-test suite over as the acceptance suite — the tests that pin drop-not-clamp behavior (NightscoutDataMapperTest, SafetyLimitsTest, the extract* driver tests) are the enforcement mechanism, since the interfaces themselves never enforced it on Android either.

risks.risk: Core Bluetooth is entirely absent from the iOS Simulator, so scanning, connecting, pairing (both styles), state restoration, connection state machines, and every driver's protocol handling are unexercisable in the primary development loop. The developer's stated intent to validate in the Simulator collides directly with the subsystem's core hardware capability.
risks.mitigation: Ship a compiled-in simulated driver as a first-class deliverable (the descendant of Android's demo glucometer plugin), so registry lifecycle, mutual exclusion, activation persistence, card rendering, settings persistence, detail screens, and the whole Nightscout path are Simulator-testable end to end. Maintain an explicit device-only test matrix covering: BLE scan/connect/pair, state restoration after background termination, Keychain accessibility while locked, local-network permission prompt, and background task cadence.

risks.risk: Several other capabilities are also invisible in the Simulator, in ways that produce works-here-fails-there bugs. BGTaskScheduler does not fire on its own schedule. The Local Network privacy prompt does not appear, so a LAN self-hosted backend can work perfectly in the Simulator and fail silently on the first device. The Simulator device is effectively always unlocked, so Keychain accessibility-class errors and data-protection failures during background operation cannot surface. App suspension semantics do not apply, so a `while true` polling loop appears to work.
risks.mitigation: Trigger background task handlers via the debugger's simulate-launch call to validate correctness in the Simulator, and reserve cadence and suspension behavior for device testing. Test the LAN backend path on device before declaring backend-optional mode done. Add a device smoke test that locks the phone and confirms background Bluetooth ingestion still writes to the Keychain and the database.

risks.risk: CBPeripheral identifiers are not stable across app reinstall and are not MAC addresses, so the persisted 'paired address' model breaks in a way Android's never does. A user who reinstalls the app finds their pump apparently unpaired even though the OS-level bond is intact — and because iOS Keychain items survive app deletion, they may simultaneously be holding stale pairing secrets for a device identifier that no longer resolves.
risks.mitigation: Model the stored identity as a UUID plus, where the protocol offers one, a stable device serial read after connect. On launch, attempt retrieval by identifier and then by connected-peripherals-with-services before falling back to a scan. Purge all driver credentials on first run after a fresh install, keyed off a UserDefaults flag (UserDefaults is wiped on deletion, Keychain is not).

risks.risk: The Nightscout paging loop has no iteration cap and no timeout on Android and persists its cursor only at loop exit. Inside a ~30-second background window, a full backfill will be killed mid-run, discard all progress, and repeat — never converging, while repeated expirations cause iOS to throttle the app's future background scheduling.
risks.mitigation: Persist the cursor after every successful page, add both a wall-clock deadline and an iteration cap, wire the expiration handler to cooperative cancellation, always report task completion, and route first-run full backfills to the foreground or a longer processing task.

risks.risk: Removing the runtime plugin path removes the only way a non-developer can try a community driver, and raises the bar for developers from an adb push to cloning, opening Xcode, and signing with their own Apple ID (7 days on a free account). Community driver contribution — an explicit goal of the Android architecture, with a documented contributor path and a reference example plugin — will slow measurably.
risks.mitigation: Make the compile-time path as frictionless as possible: one SPM package plus one line in a registration array, a documented fork-and-build guide covering signing and profile expiry, and a driver template. Ship the simulated driver as the working reference implementation the example plugin used to be. Set expectations in CONTRIBUTING that iOS drivers reach users through merge and a TestFlight build, on the maintainer's release cadence.

risks.risk: ISO-8601 date decoding will silently fail on some backend responses. Python emits fractional seconds only when non-zero, and Swift's default ISO8601 decoding strategy handles one form or the other, not both — a decode failure aborts the whole page, which the engine classifies as transient and retries forever against a condition that will never change.
risks.mitigation: Use a decoding strategy that accepts both forms, add fixture tests with and without fractional seconds, and add a distinct outcome for decode failures so they are visible as a data-contract problem rather than mimicking a network transient.

risks.risk: App Store / TestFlight review scrutiny. A diabetes app that connects to insulin pumps and displays glucose invites review under the physical-harm and health-data guidelines even for external TestFlight groups, which do go through Beta App Review. Bluetooth and background-mode entitlements plus an ATS exception in the same binary compound the attention.
risks.mitigation: Lean on what is already true and make it visible: the app is read-only monitoring with no therapeutic write anywhere in the SDK surface, which is the strongest possible answer to the physical-harm question. Carry over the existing medical disclaimer, keep the ATS exception narrow (local networking only, never arbitrary loads), justify each background mode against a concrete user-visible capability, and keep every Info.plist usage description specific rather than boilerplate. Note that TestFlight builds expire after 90 days, which sets a floor on release cadence for beta users.

risks.risk: Multiple CBCentralManager instances each carrying a restore identifier are all restored by the system at launch. A restore identifier belonging to a driver that was removed, renamed, or gated off in a later build produces phantom restorations with no owner, and the app may be relaunched in the background for a device it can no longer talk to.
risks.mitigation: Derive restore identifiers deterministically from the driver's canonical id, treat an unrecognized identifier in the restore payload as a signal to cancel the connection and stop, and log it. Never reuse a retired driver's identifier for a different driver.

risks.risk: The event bus is documented as lossy and at-most-once (256-slot buffer, drop-oldest, no replay), and the Android notes acknowledge a calibration request could be dropped under load. iOS adds a new pressure the Android design never faced: an app suspended mid-flight loses in-memory subscribers entirely, so an event published during a background wake may reach nobody.
risks.mitigation: Keep the bus for what it does today — non-critical cross-driver coordination — and hold the line that nothing safety-critical routes through it. Any alert, calibration, or persistence path must go through durable storage, not the bus. Document this constraint in the driver SDK so a future contributor does not build an alert on it.

questions_for_pm: Silent push is the only mechanism that can give the Nightscout cloud source near-real-time background updates on iOS, but it requires APNs credentials scoped to this app's Team ID and bundle ID — which a self-hoster cannot obtain, and which cannot be safely distributed to every self-hosted backend. That leaves a fork: either the project operates a first-party push relay (meaning the project runs infrastructure and holds device tokens for users who opt in, with the privacy implications that carries), or self-hosted users accept best-effort background freshness driven by app usage and Bluetooth wakes. This is a business, privacy, and infrastructure-ownership decision that neither the Android repo nor Apple's rules can settle; everything else about the background scheduling design is resolved above and does not depend on the answer.
